Welcome toA Changing Solenoid

A solenoid's current changes: is there an electric field outside it, where B is zero?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the electric field induced by a solenoid whose current changes, inside and outside it, from Faraday's law

About this simulation

On screen
The solenoid end-on, to scale out to 20 cm from the axis: the heavy circle of radius a with its anticlockwise current I, circle-dot symbols for B inside only, the solid line a and the dashed line s to the probe. While dI/dt is not zero, blue circles of E about the axis: a heavy one through the probe and faint ones where the probe was released, each with four arrowheads for the sense. A copper ring through the probe when placed. Inset: Eφ against s, drawn only where the probe has been; the previous setting's trace in grey.
Controls
dI/dt sets how fast the winding current changes; a sets the solenoid radius (changing either greys the present trace and starts a new one); drag the probe dot along the dashed line, or use the slider or its preset chips, to set s; the toggle places a wire ring at the probe radius.
Measured
All values at the instant I = 2.0 A with n = 1000 turns per metre: s in cm, B at the probe in mT, dΦB/dt through the circle of radius s in mWb/s, and Eφ at the probe in mV/m, positive anticlockwise seen from +z. These values are in the Readouts panel below the Controls.
Model
An ideal, very long solenoid: B = μ0nI inside and zero outside. The current changes slowly enough that B keeps this shape at every instant (quasi-static), and the ring's own current is too small to change the flux.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A steady current

Set the rate to 0, the radius to a = 4 cm and the probe to s = 2 cm, with no ring, so that a steady current of 2.0 A gives B = 2.51 mT inside the solenoid. Before looking at the main view and the readouts, predict the electric field at the probe.

2 · Turn up the current

Keep a = 4 cm, the probe at s = 2 cm and no ring. Before setting the rate to +100 A/s, predict the direction of the electric field at the probe, inside the solenoid. Then set the rate.

3 · From the axis to the wall

Keep the rate at +100 A/s, a = 4 cm and no ring, and drag the probe to s = 0. Before dragging it out to the wall at s = 4 cm, predict how the size of Eφ changes along the way. Then drag it there.

4 · Outside the windings

Keep the rate at +100 A/s, a = 4 cm and no ring. Before dragging the probe out to s = 8 cm, where the magnetic field is zero, predict Eφ there. Then drag it there.

5 · A narrower solenoid

Keep the rate at +100 A/s, the probe at s = 8 cm and no ring. Before changing the radius from a = 4 cm to a = 2 cm, predict Eφ at the probe. Then change it, and drag the probe in to the axis and back out to s = 8 cm to compare the new trace with the grey one.

6 · A ring as the current falls

Set the radius back to a = 4 cm, keep the rate at +100 A/s, drag the probe to s = 12 cm and place the ring, whose current then runs clockwise, opposite to the windings. Before changing the rate to −100 A/s, so that the current in the windings decreases, predict the sense of the current in the ring. Then change the rate.

7 · What the solenoid shows

A changing magnetic flux comes with a circulating electric field, ∮E·dℓ = −dΦB/dt, even where B itself is zero.

Inside the windings Eφ grows in proportion to s; outside it falls as 1/s and depends only on the total changing flux, πa2μ0n dI/dt. Its sense always opposes the change (Lenz), and a wire ring anywhere round the axis carries a current driven by it.

The Physics

A Solenoid with a Changing Current · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A long solenoid carries a current of 2.0 A, and the sim lets that current be ramped up or down. A probe sits at a distance s from the axis, inside the windings or well outside them, and the readouts report what the field is there. A wire ring can be placed through the probe.

What you'll learn

  • What decides the electric field at the probe.
  • Which way it points, and how its size depends on s.
  • What it is outside the windings, where B is zero.
  • How the solenoid's radius and the sense of the current change it.
The set-up, end-on: a solenoid of radius a, and a probe a distance s from the axis.

What's on screen

  • Main view: the solenoid end-on, to scale out to 20 cm. The heavy circle of radius a carries the winding current, and circle-dot symbols show B out of the page inside the windings only. The solid line is a, the dashed line is s.
  • Blue circles: the electric field the sim draws about the axis, with arrowheads for its sense.
  • Copper ring: the wire ring through the probe, when the toggle is on.
  • Inset: Eφ against s, drawn only where the probe has been, with the previous setting's trace in grey.
See itLook at the sim at its opening values. Watch for: the solenoid end-on with B shown inside the windings only, and Field B in the Readouts.

Fixed: the winding current at this instant is I = 2.0 A, with n = 1000 turns per metre, so B = μ0nI = 2.51 mT inside and 0 outside. The current changes slowly enough that this shape holds at every instant, and the ring's own current is too small to alter the flux. Eφ is positive anticlockwise, seen from +z.

03

Only a changing flux counts: a steady current gives no E

Faraday's law ties the circulation of E round a closed circle to the rate of change of the magnetic flux through it. The sim applies it to the circle through the probe, whose flux rate is the Flux rate readout.

∮ E·dℓ = −dΦB/dt

Faraday's law for a circle at rest; notes (7.16).

With the rate set to 0 the current is steady, so dΦB/dt is zero for every circle and Eφ = 0 at the probe. B is still 2.51 mT there. A strong field that is not changing produces no electric field.

Key idea. B does not make E. The rate of change of the flux does.
See itLeave the rate at 0, the radius at 4 cm and the probe at 2 cm. Watch for: Field B reading 2.51 mT while Flux rate and Field Eφ both read 0.000.
04

Inside the windings E circles clockwise and grows with s

Symmetry fixes the shape of E. No charge means no radial component, and the solenoid's symmetry rules out a component along the axis, so E circles the axis. For a rising current B out of the page is growing, and E circles clockwise, opposite to the winding current.

End-on, with the current rising: the circles of E run clockwise; notes Figure 64.

Eφ = −(μ0ns/2) dI/dt

Inside the windings, s < a; notes (7.18).

Inside, the enclosed flux grows as s² while the circle's length grows as s, so Eφ grows in proportion to s and is zero on the axis. At +100 A/s and a = 4 cm, Eφ = −1.257 mV/m at s = 2 cm and −2.513 mV/m at the wall. The minus sign means clockwise.

See itSet the rate to +100 A/s, keep a = 4 cm and put the probe at 2 cm. Watch for: Field Eφ reading −1.257 mV/m, and the blue circles running clockwise.
See itNow put the probe at the wall, s = 4 cm. Watch for: Field Eφ doubling to −2.513 mV/m.
05

Outside the windings E is not zero: it falls as 1/s

A circle of radius s greater than a encloses the whole changing flux, although B is zero on the circle itself. The flux rate then stays at 0.632 mWb/s for a = 4 cm and +100 A/s, however far out the probe goes, and the circle gets longer, so Eφ falls as 1/s.

Eφ = −(μ0na2/2s) dI/dt

Outside the windings, s > a; notes (7.19).
Eφ against s for a = 4 cm at +100 A/s: a straight line up to the wall, then a 1/s fall.

The wall value of −2.513 mV/m halves to −1.257 mV/m at s = 8 cm, where B reads 0.00 mT, and is −0.838 mV/m at 12 cm.

Key idea. E at a point is set by the flux through the circle that passes through it, not by B at the point.
dI/dt a s

These sliders move the sim too. The values come from the sim's own model.

See itKeep +100 A/s and a = 4 cm, and put the probe at s = 8 cm. Watch for: Field B at 0.00 mT while Field Eφ reads −1.257 mV/m.
06

A narrower solenoid gives a quarter of the field outside

Outside the windings, Eφ depends on the solenoid only through the flux it encloses, which goes as a². Halve the radius from 4 cm to 2 cm and the flux rate falls from 0.632 to 0.158 mWb/s, so at s = 8 cm Eφ falls from −1.257 to −0.314 mV/m. A radius of 6 cm gives 2.25 times the 4 cm value, −2.827 mV/m.

Eφ against s at +100 A/s for a = 4 cm and a = 2 cm. At s = 8 cm the narrow one is a quarter of the wide one.

Inside, Eφ depends only on s, so the two traces coincide up to the smaller wall at 2 cm. There the narrow solenoid turns over and falls as 1/s while the wide one keeps rising.

See itKeep +100 A/s and the probe at 8 cm, and set the radius to 2 cm. Watch for: Flux rate falling to 0.158 mWb/s and Field Eφ to −0.314 mV/m.
07

A ring follows E, and reverses when the current falls

A closed wire ring through the probe is driven round by E, so its current runs the way E circles. While the winding current rises, E is clockwise and so is the ring current. The ring's own field inside points into the page, opposing the growth of the flux, as Lenz's law requires.

The ring through the probe: its current follows E, so it opposes the change of flux.

Set the rate to −100 A/s and the flux decreases. E reverses to anticlockwise, the same sense as the winding current, and the ring's field now points out of the page, opposing the loss. At s = 12 cm, Eφ changes from −0.838 to +0.838 mV/m. The ring lies wholly where B is zero, yet it carries current.

See itPut the rate at +100 A/s, a = 4 cm, s = 12 cm and the ring on. Watch for: Field Eφ reading −0.838 mV/m, and the ring's arrowheads running clockwise.
See itNow set the rate to −100 A/s. Watch for: Field Eφ reading 0.838 mV/m, now positive, and the ring's arrowheads reversing.
08

Where it matters

  • Coupled coils. A coil wound round a solenoid is driven by the solenoid's changing flux even though B is zero where its wire lies. The notes use this for two coaxial solenoids and for the transformer.
  • E that is not conservative. This field circulates, so the voltage round a loop depends on the path. The notes write it in differential form as ∇×E = −∂B/∂t.
  • Where the model stops. It is an ideal very long solenoid with B = μ0nI inside and zero outside, and a current slow enough that this holds at each instant. Real coils are finite, and the sim does not follow fast changes.
09

Summary

In one line. The circle through the probe, the flux it encloses and how fast that flux changes together set Eφ at the probe.

Common mix-ups

  • "A strong B must come with an E." At 2.51 mT and a rate of 0, Eφ is 0.
  • "Eφ is the same at every s inside." It grows from 0 on the axis to −2.513 mV/m at the wall.
  • "Outside, where B is zero, E is zero too." At s = 8 cm, Eφ is −1.257 mV/m.
  • "A falling current drives the ring the same way." The sign of E flips: at 12 cm and −100 A/s, Eφ is +0.838 mV/m.

Things to try on your own

  • Set the rate to +50 A/s and compare Eφ at 2 cm with the +100 A/s value. Then set −50 A/s.
  • Drag the probe from the axis out to 20 cm and note where |Eφ| is largest, for a = 2, 4 and 6 cm.
